descripcion_es: Who called? versus Who did you call?: when the auxiliary do is not used.
resumen: When who, what or which ask about the subject of the sentence, do / does / did is not used and the verb is in its affirmative form (Who called?). When they ask about the object, the question has an auxiliary as usual (Who did you call?).

filas: What did the dog eat? (the cake)

explicacion.texto: Subject question: the answer is the person or thing that does the action. The question word takes the place of the subject and the word order is that of an affirmative sentence: Who lives here? What happened? Which team won?
In a subject question the verb agrees in the third person singular even if the answer is plural: Who wants coffee? (not Who want...).

items: Object question: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb: Who did you see? What does she want?
With be or with other auxiliaries, do is not added: Who is coming? / Who are you waiting for?
In object questions the preposition usually goes at the end: Who are you talking to?

ejemplos.frase: Who did you invite to the wedding?
Which bus goes to the airport?

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If who is the subject, did is not used (except for emphasis).
What is the subject of happen: no did.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Who you saw at the party?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Who did you see at the party?
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If who is the object, you need did + infinitive.
In subject questions the verb is in the third person singular.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions: when who asks about the person who does the action, do/does/did is not used and the verb is in its affirmative form. The clue is that the answer would be the subject (Messi scored the first goal), and that the object, the first goal, comes after the gap. That is why it is Who scored…?, with the verb in the past simple and no auxiliary.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Who is the subject: past verb without did.

por_opcion.scored: Correct: subject question, past verb without did.
por_opcion.did score: Incorrect in a neutral question: who is the subject and does not take did. It is only heard for emphasis or to contradict (Who did score, then?), a special use that is not what is being asked for.
por_opcion.did scored: Incorrect: besides did being unnecessary, after did the verb is never in the past.

ejercicios.frase: Who ___ at the station? — I met my cousin.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for object questions: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. The answer (I met my cousin) shows that who is the object: you met someone, and we are asking about that person. That is why it is Who did you meet…?, with did and the verb in the infinitive, without -ed, because did already marks the past.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Who is the object (you met someone): did + subject + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Con quién te encontraste en la estación? — Con mi primo.

por_opcion.you met: Incorrect: an object question needs the auxiliary did before the subject; “Who you met?” has affirmative word order.
por_opcion.did you meet: Correct: object question (you met someone), with did + subject + infinitive.
por_opcion.did you met: Incorrect: after did the verb is in the infinitive (meet); did already expresses the past, and it is not marked twice.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions: what takes the place of the subject and the verb is as in an affirmative sentence, without did. The clue is that what we are looking for is what happened, which would be the subject of the answer (An accident happened to my car). Also, happen is intransitive: it has no object, so it can never form an object question. That is why it is What happened…?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: What is the subject: no did.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Qué le ha pasado a tu coche?

por_opcion.did happen: Incorrect: what is the subject and does not take did (except in a very special emphatic use).
por_opcion.happened: Correct: subject question, verb in the past simple without an auxiliary.
por_opcion.did it happen: Incorrect: it adds an unnecessary subject it, because the subject is already what.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card that in a subject question the verb agrees in the third person singular, even if the answer may be plural. The clue is that who is the subject (we are asking who speaks) and the verb is in the present, so it takes -s: Who speaks…? Does is not added because it is a subject question.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Subject question in the present: third person singular.

por_opcion.speak: Incorrect: who as subject agrees in the third person singular: speaks.
por_opcion.speaks: Correct: subject question in the present, with third-person -s.
por_opcion.does speak: Incorrect in a neutral question: does is not used in subject questions.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the question with the verb in the past simple (without an auxiliary if it is not needed).
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions: who asks about the author, who would be the subject of the answer (Cervantes wrote Don Quixote). That is why the verb is in the past simple without did, in its affirmative form. Write is irregular and its past is wrote. The instruction warns you: without an auxiliary if it is not needed.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Who is the subject: did is not used. The correct form is Who wrote…?
Write is irregular: its past is wrote.
Written is the past participle; without have, the past is wrote.

ejercicios.frase: What ___ you have for dinner yesterday?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for object questions: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. The clue is that the sentence already has a subject, you, so what asks about the object (what you ate). As the tense is past (yesterday) and the verb have is in the base form, the auxiliary is did: What did you have for dinner?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Object question in the past: did.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Yesterday indicates the past: the auxiliary is did.
Here have is the main verb (to eat); the question also needs the auxiliary did.
Had does not work as an auxiliary with the infinitive have; you need did.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for object questions and the note in the card that the preposition usually goes at the end (Who are you talking to?). The clue is that the sentence already has a subject, your sister, and who asks about the person she works with. As the tense is present and the subject is third person, the auxiliary is does, and the verb stays in the base form, work.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Object question in the present with a third-person subject: does.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Your sister is third person singular: does.
Is forms the present continuous with -ing (is working); with the base form work you need does.
There is no sign of the past; the sentence is about a habitual present: does.

ejercicios.enunciado: Make a question with who about the person who does the action (Laura).
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions: if you ask about the person who does the action (Laura), who takes her place and the rest of the sentence stays the same, without did. The clue is the instruction: Laura is the one who sends, that is, the subject. You just replace Laura with Who and keep sent the email: Who sent the email?

errores_previstos.explicacion: Did is not used in a subject question; the verb is in the past: Who sent…?
This is an object question (what or who did Laura send?), not a question about the person who sent it.
Send is irregular: its past is sent.

ejercicios.enunciado: Make a question with who about the person who receives the action (Javier).
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for object questions: who + did + subject + infinitive. The clue is the instruction: you are asking about Javier, who receives the action (the object), while Laura is still the subject. That is why you need did, and called goes back to the base form call. Whom is also accepted; it is the formal object form, but in spoken English who is normal.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Object question: who + did + subject + infinitive.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This question has who as the subject: it asks who called Laura, not who she called.
After did the verb is in the infinitive: call.
A literal translation of Spanish “¿a quién?”: call takes a direct object, with no preposition.

ejercicios.enunciado: Make a question with what about the cause (the noise).
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions: the noise is the subject (what woke you), so what replaces it and did is not used. The clue is the instruction, which asks about the cause, the noise, which comes before the verb in the original sentence. Also, me changes to you because the question is now addressed to the other person: What woke you up?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The noise is the subject: what + verb, without did.

errores_previstos.explicacion: What is the subject: did is not used. The correct form is What woke you up?
The question is addressed to the other person: me must change to you.
This question takes you as the subject and changes the meaning (“what did you wake?”).

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions: who asks about who won, which is the subject, so it does not take did. The mistake in the sentence comes from overgeneralising the rule that past questions take did. The clue is that the answer would be the subject (The Labour Party won the election). That is why the verb is in the past simple: won, the irregular past of win.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Who is the subject: no did.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: did is not needed in a subject question (it would only be used for special emphasis).
Did has been removed but the verb has been left in the present; the past of win is won.
Win is irregular: its past is won.

ejercicios.frase: What you want for your birthday?
respuestas: What do you want for your birthday?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for object questions: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. The clue is that the sentence has a subject, you, and what asks about the object (what you want). As the tense is present and the subject is you, the auxiliary is do: What do you want…? Without an auxiliary, the sentence keeps affirmative word order and is incorrect.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Object question in the present: do is missing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What you want for your birthday?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the object question is missing the auxiliary do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What does you want for your birthday?
errores_previstos.explicacion: With you the auxiliary is do, not does.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What want you for your birthday?
errores_previstos.explicacion: In modern English the main verb is not inverted; you need do: What do you want?

ejercicios.frase: Who want a cup of tea?
respuestas: Who wants a cup of tea?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card that in subject questions the verb agrees in the third person singular, even if the answer may be plural (Who wants coffee?). The clue is that who is the subject and the verb is in the present. That is why want becomes wants. Even if we expect several people to answer, the form is singular.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In subject questions the verb is in the third person singular.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Who want a cup of tea?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: with who as the subject, the verb takes -s.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Who does want a cup of tea?
errores_previstos.explicacion: In a subject question, does is not added.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Who do want a cup of tea?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Neither do nor does: a subject question has no auxiliary and the verb takes -s.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words in order to make a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for object questions and the note in the card that the preposition usually goes at the end: Who are you talking to? The clue is that you is the subject and who is the object of the preposition to (you talked to someone), so you need did. The order is Who + did + you + talk + to. Putting the preposition first (To whom did you talk?) is very formal and is not what is practised here.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Object question with the preposition at the end.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A literal translation of Spanish “¿con quién?”: in English the preposition normally goes at the end; it goes first only in a formal register and with whom.
The auxiliary did goes before the subject: Who did you talk to.
The subject you goes between did and the verb: did you talk.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words in order to make a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule for subject questions with which + noun: which team takes the place of the subject and the word order is affirmative, without did. The clue is that you are asking about the team that won, that is, about the subject, and that there is no auxiliary among the words. That is why it is Which team won the league?

errores_previstos.explicacion: Which and its noun form a block: which team, and then the verb.
This copies an order with the object first: in the question, which team goes at the beginning.
The word order of a subject question is that of an affirmative sentence: subject + verb + object.

descripcion_larga_es: When who, what or which ask about the subject (the person or thing that does the action), the question does not take do, does or did and keeps the word order of an affirmative sentence: Who called? When they ask about the object, it does take an auxiliary: Who did you call? It is difficult for Spanish speakers because in Spanish both questions are formed in the same way and because, after learning that questions take do, they put it in all of them.

contexto.que_es: These are two types of question with who, what or which. In a subject question the question word takes the place of the subject and the verb is as in an affirmative sentence (Who wrote this?). In an object question the question word replaces the complement and the question follows the usual structure with an auxiliary (What did she write?).
contexto.por_que_importa: The difference changes the meaning: Who called Tom? asks who called, and Who did Tom call? asks who Tom called. Also, putting did in a subject question (“Who did win?”) or leaving it out of an object question (“What you want?”) are very noticeable mistakes. In an oral exam, asking “What happened?” or “Who told you?” naturally makes you sound fluent.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Use a subject question when we do not know who or what did something: Who won?, What happened?, Which team scored? Use an object question when we know who acts and are looking for the complement: Who did you meet? The signal is to ask yourself whether the answer would be the subject of the sentence. In Spanish there is no difference in form (“¿quién llamó?”, “¿a quién llamaste?”), except for the preposition a.
